stories.title: RS-71 or SR-71?
stories.dek: The best-known story about the Blackbird's name says a president fumbled two letters; his own recording says otherwise.
stories.verdict: Johnson did not garble the name. The official transcript and the White House recording have him say "SR-71" every time he names the aircraft, and a printed copy of the statement from August 1964 agrees. "RS-71" was a real name in Washington that summer: a senator used it on the Senate floor five days later, and a congressman was still using it in 1965. The claim that the President swapped the letters first appears, in the earliest dated source this project has found, in the CIA's Archangel of 2007, which gives no source for it. The Air Force's own account says the designation was changed to SR before the speech and that press material still carried RS-71. No draft of the statement or press handout reading RS-71 has yet been found to settle which account is right.

body.text: At half past three on the afternoon of Friday 24 July 1964, in the State Department Auditorium, Lyndon Johnson opened his twenty-third news conference with an aeroplane. He announced "a major new strategic manned aircraft system" for Strategic Air Command, built around "the new SR-71 aircraft", which would fly at more than three times the speed of sound and above 80,000 feet. The billion-dollar program, he said, had begun in February 1963. Then he turned to record farm exports.

The story told about that moment ever since is that the Air Force had called the aircraft the RS-71, for reconnaissance and strike, and that Johnson read the letters backwards. Rather than correct the President, the story goes, the Air Force kept his version and created a strategic reconnaissance category to fit it. The CIA's own history of the A-12, David Robarge's Archangel, tells it in just those terms: Johnson "mistakenly transposed the designator letters", and "Air Force officials let the error stand".

The record of the day does not bear this out. The official transcript has Johnson say "SR-71" every time he names the aircraft, and in the same statement he speaks of the RS-70, a different aircraft reviewed by the Joint Chiefs, with its letters in their proper order. The White House Communications Agency recording of the conference, now at the LBJ Library, has "SR-71" about 34 seconds in, again at 58 seconds and once more at 1 minute 39 seconds. A printed copy of the statement that the CIA filed on 3 August 1964 reads "SR-71" as well, and the next morning's New York Herald Tribune glossed the letters for its readers as "Strategic Reconnaissance".

Yet RS-71 was not invented later. On 29 July, five days after the announcement, Senator Gordon Allott of Colorado told the Senate that the President had announced a new plane "which I believe is now designated as the RS-71", and went on to object that a billion dollars for this "new RS-71 plane, formerly known as the A-11" had been hidden in the defence budget. The confusion lasted. In closed House Armed Services Committee hearings reported by Aviation Week in May 1965, the chairman asked about the "SR-71", the Air Force Chief of Staff, Gen. John P. McConnell, answered "YF-12", and Representative William H. Bates offered "RS-71".

Behind the secrecy the aircraft had already worn several names. Lockheed's two-seat development of the A-12 was the R-12, and Air Force officials were interested in a reconnaissance and strike variant, the RS-12, which, in NASA historian Peter Merlin's words, was "eventually re-designated SR-71". CIA memoranda called the Air Force aircraft the R-12 in December 1962 and still did so in August 1964, a month after the President had given it a public name. Archangel says the Air Force's first six were ordered as RS-71s.

The Air Force tells it differently. A 2014 history note from the 9th Reconnaissance Wing at Beale says that the Chief of Staff, Gen. Curtis LeMay, preferred SR for strategic reconnaissance, that the designation was changed before the speech, and that the media transcripts still carried RS-71, "thus creating the rumor that the president misread" it. That account fits the transcript and the recording, and it would explain why RS-71 lingered on Capitol Hill. But it cites no document, and it puts the announcement a day late, on 25 July.

Each part of the story can be dated. "SR-71" is in the President's own words on the day and in the transcript published from them. "RS-71" is on the Senate floor within the week. The claim that joins them, that the President swapped the letters, is the one that travelled, yet the earliest dated telling this project has found is the CIA's web edition of Archangel, posted in October 2007 without a source and repeated unchanged in the 2012 edition.

differ.text: Two official accounts disagree. The CIA's Archangel (web edition 2007; second edition 2012, p. 53) says Johnson transposed the letters and the Air Force let the error stand. The 9th Reconnaissance Wing's 2014 history note says Gen. Curtis LeMay had the designation changed to SR-71 before the speech and that media transcripts still read RS-71. Neither cites a document. The same Air Force note dates the announcement 25 July 1964; the transcript places the news conference at 3:30 p.m. on Friday 24 July 1964. Internal names also differ: CIA memoranda use R-12, Merlin traces R-12 and RS-12 to SR-71, and Archangel says the first contract was for six RS-71s.

stories.title: Six missiles over Hanoi
stories.dek: On 30 October 1967 North Vietnam fired a salvo of SA-2s at Dennis Sullivan's A-12; he flew on through them, and a sliver of metal came home lodged beside a fuel tank.

body.text: By the autumn of 1967 the CIA's A-12s had been flying BLACK SHIELD missions from Kadena, Okinawa, for five months, photographing North Vietnam for any sign of surface-to-surface missiles. They crossed it at Mach 3.1 to 3.2 and a little above 80,000 feet, and on the first fifteen missions nobody fired at them. That changed on 28 October, on the 16th mission, when a single SA-2 rose toward Dennis Sullivan in Article 131 (60-6937). It was launched too late, and the aircraft was already beyond its reach.

Two days later Sullivan was back over the North in Article 129 (60-6932) on mission BX6734, the 18th of the operation. He left Kadena at 0219 GMT on 30 October to make two photographic passes. On the first, radar tracked him and two missile sites made ready but did not fire. On the second, heading for Hanoi from the west at Mach 3.1 and 84,000 feet, his jammers began answering FAN SONG guidance radars from at least six sites at once, as battalions of two North Vietnamese missile regiments tried to engage him.

Sullivan raised his rear-view periscope. His report, quoted in the CIA's later analysis, described missiles "in a steep climb through the aircraft altitude of approximately 83,500 feet" that pushed over, levelled off and "guided toward the stern of the aircraft to detonation." He counted at least six contrails and three detonations, all behind him, and saw one missile climbing 100 to 200 yards off his right side, abeam the cockpit. Fourteen seconds of mission photography caught six vapour trails.

He landed at Kadena at 0603 GMT, 3 hours 44 minutes after take-off, and the mission was graded a success. The ground crew then found a single hole, "approximately the size which would have been made by a 30.06 shell", in a fillet just aft of the right main landing gear. Whatever made it had passed through the skin and two metal supports, one of them for a fuel tank, and stopped in the structure around the number five tank. It went to Washington by courier, and the analysts judged it debris from a missile, not part of a warhead.

The CIA's analysts later counted at least seven and possibly ten missiles launched during the mission, six to nine of them on the second pass. They suspected the North Vietnamese had moved missile battalions into the Hanoi area to mass fire on a route the A-12s had flown before, and had tried to spoof or saturate the jammers. Even so, they judged the SA-2's chance against an A-12 with its jammers working to be "essentially zero". Kadena saw it differently: one officer reported the pilots "showing considerable anxiety about overflying this area", and Richard Helms suspended the missions. None flew until 8 December, and that one went to the Cambodia-Laos border area; flights over North Vietnam resumed on 15 December, the first two on different routes.

It was the only time enemy fire damaged an A-12. One more missile was fired at an A-12, on 4 January 1968, and burst well over a mile away. Article 129 itself was lost with Jack Weeks over the Pacific in June 1968. The fragments outlived it: in 2013 the CIA announced that it had acquired them, together with the damaged section of the aircraft, a hole torn through its centre, for display in its museum.

differ.text: The records do not agree on the details. The 6 November 1967 memo describes a single hole made by one "pellet"; McIninch and the 27 November analysis call it one piece of debris that was not a warhead pellet; the CIA's 2013 museum story speaks of two small pieces of metal and shows two fragments. Archangel and McIninch say at least six missiles were fired, while the 27 November analysis counts at least seven and possibly ten over the whole mission. The 2013 story says flights over North Vietnam stopped for two months; Archangel's dates (no mission until 8 December, none over the North until 15 December) make it about six weeks.

stories.title: Titanium from the enemy?
stories.dek: The spy plane built to overfly the Soviet Union was supposedly made of Soviet metal bought through front companies; the CIA's own files from the time tell a plainer story.
stories.verdict: Unproven, and unlikely for the A-12. The CIA's records from 1960 and 1961 name Titanium Metals Corporation as the supplier and describe a problem of quality, not of quantity. The United States had spare sponge capacity and large government stockpiles, while the Soviet Union was itself trying to buy titanium abroad. In the sources checked, the Soviet-metal story first appears in Ben Rich's memoir of 1994, three decades after the purchases; the CIA's 2007 history repeats it on Rich's word alone, and later versions add details, such as rutile ore and front companies for pizza ovens, that no document supports. Soviet sponge was sold in the West from the mid-1960s, so a purchase for later SR-71 production cannot be ruled out, but no record of one has been found. Say that Rich claimed it; never say that much, or all, of the Blackbirds' titanium was Soviet.

body.text: One of the best Blackbird stories holds that the aircraft built to spy on the Soviet Union was made of Soviet metal. Ben Rich, Lockheed's lead propulsion engineer on the A-12, put it in print in 1994 in a memoir written with Leo Janos. He wrote that the supplier, Titanium Metals Corporation, had "only limited reserves of the precious alloy", so the CIA searched the world and, "using third parties and dummy companies", bought the base metal from one of the world's leading exporters, the Soviet Union, without the Russians ever suspecting what it was for.

Titanium was the only practical answer to the heat. Most of the A-12's skin would run at 500 to 600 F, so Lockheed built over 90 percent of the airframe from a titanium alloy nearly as strong as stainless steel at half the weight; across the Blackbird family titanium alloys made up 93 percent of the structural weight, and Lockheed made more than 13 million titanium parts over 20 years. The early trouble was quality. The CIA's first in-house history (1970-71) records that some 80 percent of the early deliveries from Titanium Metals Corporation had to be rejected, and that supply became consistently satisfactory only in 1961, after a delegation from headquarters visited the company to explain the program's priority.

The agency's files from those years are about quality and secrecy, not Moscow. On 13 January 1960 John Parangosky, deputy chief of the CIA's Development Branch, sent the project's cover officer a trade-press item putting 1959 titanium mill shipments at 3,100 tons, and asked whether Lockheed's planned titanium purchases raised "any cover problems", since production seemed to be closely watched. On 19 April 1961 CIA officers met an official of Titanium Metals Corporation about late deliveries. Their record blames strict quality control and high rejection rates, the time the company needed to learn to process titanium to OXCART specifications, and processing that shuttled metal between its plants. The company promised to fill every outstanding Lockheed order by 1 August 1961, and the memo notes that it was the only supplier Lockheed had found capable of the most complex titanium work.

Kelly Johnson told the same story in 1981. He wrote of working with "our supplier, Titanium Metals Corporation" when the first heat-treated parts came out so brittle that a piece knocked off a desk shattered on the floor, a problem cured by rebuilding Lockheed's acid-pickling line as a copy of the one at the company's mills. His only mention of the USSR in that section is that it had more and larger forging presses than America. Rich's sentence begins with Johnson's words, then goes where Johnson never did. The CIA's 1992 history of the U-2 and OXCART programs, written from the agency's records, also names Titanium Metals Corporation and says nothing of Soviet metal; nor does NASA historian Peter Merlin's 2009 paper.

National figures leave little room for a shortage of raw metal. In 1961, the Bureau of Mines reported, three American firms, among them Titanium Metals Corporation at Henderson, Nevada, produced 6,700 tons of titanium sponge; imports of 2,490 tons came almost entirely from Japan, with small lots from Canada and Britain; and government stockpiles held another 31,007 tons of sponge. Australia produced 88 percent of the world's rutile. A CIA economic study of 1964 found that American sponge capacity had reached about 25,000 metric tons a year, while output had fallen below 4,000 tons in 1959 after bomber cancellations. A Soviet journal admitted in 1962 that production "still lagged behind requirements", and in April 1961 Moscow had made its first approach to buy Japanese titanium, having planned to buy from Britain.

Soviet titanium did reach Western buyers later. CIA analysts reported in 1985 that Soviet exports of sponge and scrap grew from several hundred tons a year in the mid-1960s to a peak of 7,700 tons in 1974, with the United States and West Germany the leading customers. The CIA's own history of the A-12, David Robarge's Archangel (2007, revised 2012), adopted Rich's version, saying some of the scarce base metal "had to be obtained covertly" from the Soviet Union, with Rich's memoir as its only citation. A 2023 National Interest article quotes former SR-71 pilot Col. Richard Graham as saying that America lacked rutile ore and got it from the USSR by "working through Third World countries and bogus operations", one of them, it reports him saying, a front for pizza ovens.

differ.text: Sources disagree on the early rejection rate: Archangel gives 95 percent, in a sentence footnoted to Rich, while McIninch says some 80 percent and Pedlow and Welzenbach up to 80 percent. They also disagree on what was supposedly bought. Rich says base metal from one of the world's leading exporters; Robarge turns this into the country with "the largest known reserves"; Graham, as quoted in 2023, says rutile ore, although Australia then produced 88 percent of the world's rutile and, by the CIA's account, the Soviet industry chose its own low-grade ilmenite over foreign rutile. Claims that Soviet titanium output dwarfed America's are true of the 1980s (the CIA estimated about 71,000 metric tons in 1984, more than five times US output) but not of the A-12 years, when it estimated that the USSR turned about 5,000 metric tons of sponge into mill products in 1963 against American sponge production of 7,200 tons.

stories.title: Thrown clear at Mach 3.18
stories.dek: Bill Weaver never pulled his ejection handle. His SR-71 came apart around him at 78,000 feet, and he woke up falling.

body.text: On 25 January 1966 SR-71A 61-7952 took off from Edwards Air Force Base on a Lockheed test flight. Bill Weaver, a Lockheed test pilot, was in the front seat; behind him was Jim Zwayer, a Lockheed flight test specialist in reconnaissance and navigation systems. They were to evaluate those systems and to try flying with the centre of gravity further aft than normal, which cut trim drag at high Mach but made the aircraft less stable in pitch.

Weaver's own account describes what happened after they refuelled and turned east. At Mach 3.2 and 78,000 ft the right inlet's automatic control failed and he switched it to manual. In a planned 35-degree bank to the right the right inlet unstarted; the aircraft rolled further right and pitched up, and full left and forward stick did nothing. He wrote that he did not think an ejection at Mach 3.18 and 78,800 ft was survivable, and tried to tell Zwayer to stay with the aircraft, but the g-forces garbled his words.

He later learned that only two or three seconds passed between the unstart and the loss of control. He blacked out, and the SR-71 disintegrated around him. A reconstruction published by The X-Hunters, an aviation archaeology group, says the airframe failed at the main joint just ahead of the wings. The CIA's accident summary records that the pilot was "forcibly ripped from seat through lap belt and shoulder harness by wind and pressure forces" as the aircraft broke up.

Weaver wrote that he came to thinking he was dreaming, then that he must be dead, and that being dead did not seem so bad. He was falling, blind behind an iced-over face plate, his pressure suit inflated by the emergency oxygen in his seat kit. He was falling steadily rather than tumbling, so he reasoned that the small stabilising parachute had opened, and as he groped for the D-ring his main parachute opened by itself. Holding up the face plate, whose latch had broken, he saw a second parachute about a quarter of a mile away.

He landed in northeastern New Mexico, about 1.5 miles from the ranch house of Albert Mitchell Jr., who had watched the parachutes come down and flew out in his helicopter. Weaver found his lap belt and shoulder harness, shredded but still latched, hanging around him: his ejection seat had never left the aircraft. Mitchell flew to the other parachute and came back with the news that Zwayer was dead, apparently from a broken neck suffered in the break-up, then flew Weaver about 60 miles to the hospital at Tucumcari.
cite: passage beginning "The citizens of Buyeros and Albert"

body.text: The CIA's accident summary, prepared on 11 January 1967, puts the crash 107 nautical miles from Cannon Air Force Base on a bearing of 350 degrees, with wreckage strewn over an area about 16 miles long and 5 miles wide, and gives the primary cause as fuel distribution that left an unsafe centre of gravity. The accident board asked for the sharp edges on lap belt adjusters to be removed, for face plate heating during free fall and for a study of automatic ejection in a high-altitude break-up. Weaver wrote that the flight was repeated in the SR-71 simulator at Beale the next day with the same outcome, and that testing with an aft centre of gravity was stopped.
Two weeks later Weaver was back in an SR-71, flying the first sortie of a new aircraft at Palmdale. Zwayer remains the only person killed in an SR-71.

differ.text: Weaver gives Mach 3.18 and 78,800 ft at the moment of the unstart; The X-Hunters give Mach 3.17 and nearly 78,000 ft. The CIA summary puts the debris over about 16 by 5 miles, while Weaver and The X-Hunters say 15 by 10 miles. The CIA summary records Zwayer's death as a "fatal ejection" and says the manner in which his seat was fired is unknown, whereas Weaver wrote that both men were ripped out of the airplane. The summary names an unsafe centre of gravity as the primary cause; Weaver describes the cumulative effect of the inlet malfunction, reduced stability, the turn and the speed.

stories.title: New York to the Suez Canal and back
stories.dek: In October 1973 the White House wanted to see the war for itself, and the SR-71 it sent flew there and back from New York in eleven hours, refuelling six times on the way.

body.text: On the morning of 9 October 1973, three days after Egyptian and Syrian forces attacked Israeli positions in Sinai and on the Golan Heights, Henry Kissinger held a principals-only meeting of the Washington Special Actions Group in the White House Situation Room, with Defense Secretary James Schlesinger, Deputy Secretary of State Kenneth Rush, Admiral Thomas Moorer of the Joint Chiefs and William Colby of the CIA. Israel had called all night for supplies. When Schlesinger said they needed to know about the bridges, Kissinger answered, in the words of the meeting record: "We should fly the SR-71." Before the group broke up, Moorer asked whether the paperwork could be done.

On 11 October the Joint Chiefs ordered Strategic Air Command to send SR-71s to Griffiss Air Force Base, New York, and two SR-71As of the 9th Strategic Reconnaissance Wing came from Beale, California. A Middle East plan, GIANT REACH, already existed: the SR-71 would take off from Beale and land after the mission at a base whose name, like the reason it could not be used, is still blacked out in the declassified SAC chronology. Either way, SAC had to plan round trips from the United States, which doubled the tanker force. Two CIA U-2s, deployed on 7 and 8 October to be ready to cover the war, were never tasked.

The first sortie left Griffiss at 0600 GMT on 13 October, flown by Lt. Col. James Shelton with Lt. Col. Gary Coleman as reconnaissance systems officer. Reaching the targets took three air refuellings, over the Gulf of Saint Lawrence, at a point still withheld and south of Crete; three more, south of Crete, off Portugal and over the Gulf of Saint Lawrence, brought the aircraft back to Griffiss at 1713 GMT. The flight lasted 11 hours 13 minutes, beating the SR-71's endurance record of 10 hours 30 minutes from April 1971, and needed 14 KC-135Q tankers. Shelton described the mission and its six refuellings in a talk at the Western Museum of Flight, posted in 2016.

On 16 October Colby brought prints to the Situation Room. "They flew right down the Canal," he said. Taken on Saturday 13 October, they showed the Egyptians across the canal to about 8 km, as the Israelis had claimed, and nothing to support claims of huge tank losses, though Moorer warned that a shell through an engine would not show. But when Colby asked about the next flight, Kissinger demurred: the Egyptians, he said, had "been very restrained about it". The meeting put the second mission on hold.
cite: Document 191, summary of conclusions and pp. 546 to 552, with footnote 4

body.text: Colby wanted another flight "around ceasefire time" as a baseline, and on 24 October the group agreed one should run down the canal and over Egypt; Kissinger asked only whether it could avoid Cairo. At lunch he remarked that if anyone complained about the next day's flight, Washington could say it was "to fix the ceasefire lines". On 25 October Capt. Eldon Joersz and Capt. John Fuller flew it, refuelling south of Nova Scotia, north of the Azores and south of Crete, and launched and landed at the same times as the first crew. On 31 October Moorer, citing evidence of Scud missiles in Egypt, asked for a third; after an overcast delay, on 4 November Capt. Robert Helt and Capt. Larry Elliott flew 11 hours 22 minutes, the longest SR-71 flight yet.
cite: pp. 2 to 3 (PDF pp. 3 to 4), entries for 25 October and 4 November

body.text: The round trips were costly: on 6 November Vice Admiral John Weinel, for the Joint Chiefs, put a flight from New York at about half a million dollars, against $175,000 to $200,000 from Europe; on 29 November Moorer added that each used 230,000 gallons of fuel. With fuel due to reach RAF Mildenhall in England on 1 January, the group agreed on one more flight from the United States and later ones from Britain. By then, according to a veterans' timeline published by Roadrunners Internationale, GIANT REACH had moved on 15 November to Seymour Johnson Air Force Base, North Carolina.
cite: Document 364, summary of conclusions and p. 1009

body.text: The flights outlasted the fighting. Under the Egyptian-Israeli disengagement of January 1974, the United States told both governments it would photograph the disengagement areas about every ten days to two weeks and give each side the pictures. When Colby asked on 22 January whether the U-2 would do, Kissinger replied: "I told them SR-71." The Roadrunners timeline counts nine GIANT REACH sorties, the last on 6 April 1974. The CIA was then tasked to watch the disengagement areas with U-2s, and its detachment reached its still-redacted base on 21 April.

differ.text: The SAC chronology dates the first sortie 13 October, and the editors of Foreign Relations date the photographs shown on 16 October to the same day, but on 1 November Kissinger told Golda Meir that the SR-71 had photographed only twice, on the 12th and the 25th. Written on 12 December 1973, the chronology records three sorties (13 and 25 October, 4 November). On 29 November Moorer told the group that the last flight had been on 18 November, whereas the Roadrunners timeline, which credits its entries to SR-71 veteran Buddy Brown, lists a sortie on 11 November and none on 18 November, and counts nine in all to April 1974. The airframe serials (61-7979 for the first three sorties, 61-7964 on 11 November and 2 December) come only from that timeline. The chronology spells the third RSO's name Elliot.
